prompt: Explain the Air Quality Index and what the numbers mean.
hook: One number, six categories, real health stakes.

card.oneLiner: The Air Quality Index condenses pollutant levels into a single 0-500 score, with categories that run from good to severe.
keyPoints: There are six categories, each with a colour code.
The index reports the worst-performing pollutant as the dominant one.
Particulate matter usually drives the worst readings.
Each band carries health advice for the public.

framework.name: Central Pollution Control Board
framework.gloss: Method for computing the index and its categories.

whatYouCanDo: Check the AQI before outdoor exercise.
Note which pollutant is dominant, not just the number.
Use masks and air purifiers sensibly on severe days.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. The index is a communication tool, not a full health assessment.

prompt: Explain what PM2.5 is and why it is so harmful.
hook: The smallest particles do the most damage.

card.oneLiner: PM2.5 are particles smaller than 2.5 microns that penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream, making them the most damaging common air pollutant.
keyPoints: Their small size lets them bypass the body's filters.
They come from combustion, industry, vehicles and dust.
Long-term exposure is linked to heart and lung disease.
Weather can concentrate or disperse them.

framework.name: Central Pollution Control Board
framework.gloss: National standards and monitoring of fine particulate matter.

framework.name: WHO Air Quality Guidelines
framework.gloss: Health-based guideline levels for particulate matter.

whatYouCanDo: Track PM2.5 separately from the composite index.
Reduce exposure on high days, especially for children and the elderly.
Support clean fuel and transport measures near you.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Health effects depend on exposure, duration and individual factors.

prompt: Explain why north India's air quality collapses in winter.
hook: It is never just one cause.

card.oneLiner: Winter smog in north India comes from a mix of vehicle and industrial emissions, crop-residue burning, dust, and weather that traps pollution near the ground.
keyPoints: Cool air near the surface traps warmer air and pollutants above.
Low winds let pollution accumulate over days.
Crop-residue burning adds smoke in the harvest season.
Pollution travels across state boundaries.

framework.name: Central Pollution Control Board
framework.gloss: Monitoring of pollutants across the region.

framework.name: India Meteorological Department
framework.gloss: Wind and temperature conditions that affect dispersion.

whatYouCanDo: Understand that stubble burning is one source among several.
Support regional, not just city-level, action.
Watch official forecasts during the winter months.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Source apportionment varies between cities and years.

prompt: Explain crop-residue burning and what can replace it.
hook: Banning burning is easier than solving it.

card.oneLiner: Farmers often burn crop residue to clear fields quickly, and the alternatives are machines and practices that manage residue without fire.
keyPoints: Burning is quick and cheap before the next sowing.
Residue-management machines can sow through leftover stubble.
Diversified cropping and residue markets reduce the need to burn.
Incentives and timing shape whether farmers switch.

framework.name: Crop Residue Management scheme
framework.gloss: Subsidies for machines that manage stubble.

whatYouCanDo: Recognise that farmers face a short window to sow.
Avoid blaming one group for a regional problem.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. Adoption depends on cost, subsidies and local conditions.

sources.title: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

prompt: Explain the Commission for Air Quality Management and its graded response.
hook: One body now coordinates the whole region.

card.oneLiner: The Commission for Air Quality Management coordinates air-quality action across Delhi-NCR and neighbouring states, triggering graded restrictions as pollution worsens.
keyPoints: It covers a region, not a single city.
A graded response escalates restrictions stage by stage.
Measures range from dust control to curbs on vehicles and construction.
Enforcement across state boundaries remains a challenge.

framework.name: Commission for Air Quality Management Act, 2021
framework.gloss: Statutory body for air quality in the NCR region.

framework.name: Graded Response Action Plan
framework.gloss: Pre-defined measures tied to pollution levels.

whatYouCanDo: Know which GRAP stage is in force where you live.
Understand that lasting improvement needs year-round action.
card.caveats: Educational information, not professional advice. The graded plan is revised over time.
